false_hood: The False Hood That sense of truthness being false. Is like Solipsism on reverse. The numbers of “visits” from Hong Kong, Japan and others from the last review , are false. :’( The Dragon doesn’t care about it. Naturally, how could I reach the Dragon? Maybe they see it offensive, while Chinese cultures say the same about Monkeys. What issue they see in me that exist on them? Me imagining of having thousen of visits and all those inputs where just attacks :-) The comfort of a number A statistic is a story that arrives already finished. It does not ask for interpretation, it does not hesitate, and it never explains itself. That is why it is so easy to believe: believing costs nothing, while checking costs an evening with the logs. I believed the number because I wanted the number. Somebody in Hong Kong, somebody in Japan, reading the pages of a small blog written in Portugal. It is a beautiful idea, and a beautiful idea is the easiest thing in the world to accept. Solipsism, but backwards Solipsism says that only my mind exists. The reverse would be a world where everything exists except my own judgement, where the evidence is always external and always right. That is the position I fell into: the tool said thousands of visits, so there were thousands of visits, and my own eyes looking at the same logs did not count. The correction is uncomfortable and useful. The numbers were real, the visitors were not. What the dashboard counted was a crowd of scripts, each one a request, none of them a reader. What is left after the correction Not much, and that is the point. A handful of addresses that return on the same days, a few pages opened more than once, a sentence in an email from someone who actually read the text. That is the entire audience of this blog, and it is enough, because those numbers are checkable. Being wrong is good. It means there is something left to learn, and the lesson here is cheaper than most: trust the log, not the summary.
fireJail: FIELD TECHNICAL MANUAL • FIREJAIL // ZERO → PARANOID HERO • READ IN ORDER — EACH LEVEL LOCKS THE NEXT FJ ☠ 0.9.x Firejail — The Paranoid Operator's Manual SUID sandbox • namespaces • seccomp-bpf • netfilter • D-Bus • X11 • profiles • file contexts | single-file edition, no externals, vanilla JS+CSS3 only LEVEL 0 Ignition — your first jail in 60 seconds CLEARANCE: RECRUIT • NO PRIVILEGES ASSUMED 0.1 What Firejail actually is Firejail is a SUID sandbox launcher for Linux. It runs as root for a few milliseconds — just long enough to build a cage from kernel primitives — then drops privilege and executes your program as you. The cage is not emulation: it is the Linux kernel itself (namespaces, seccomp-bpf, capabilities, raqm, AppArmor/Landlock hooks) told to lie to one process tree. 🧠 Mental model: Firejail = mount namespace (fake filesystem) + PID/UTS/IPC namespaces (fake identity) + optional net/user namespaces + seccomp-bpf (forbidden syscalls) + capabilities + no_new_privs (no escalation) + profile (which rules apply). Lose any layer and you are weaker — that is why this manual is paranoid at every level. Install & first run # Debian / Ubuntu / Mint sudo apt install firejail firetools # firetools = optional Qt GUI firejail --version # The hello-world of sandboxing: firejail firefox firejail --private vlc firejail --net=none --private evince secret.pdf # Who is jailed right now? firemon --list --tree firemon --seccomp --caps --netstats ⚠️ SUID warning (read twice): firejail is installed setuid-root. On a true multi-user shell server, any SUID binary widens attack surface. Upstream advises thinking hard before deploying it there. On a single-user laptop/desktop — the target of this manual — the trade-off is overwhelmingly worth it. Try it: fake terminal (type help ) operator@paranoid: ~ — firejail sim Type `help` and press Enter. Try: firejail firefox | firejail --net=none vlc | firemon --list | firecfg --list $ 💡 This terminal is simulated with vanilla JS — no backend. It teaches syntax before you touch a real shell. 0.2 Benefits — why bother? Threat Without Firejail With Firejail (this manual) Malicious PDF / font exploit Reads ~/.ssh , ~/.gnupg , wallets private-tmp + whitelist ~/Docs + net none → sees almost nothing Browser 0-day Full home + webcam + D-Bus + network seccomp + noroot + dbus-user none + x11 + netfilter → contained Proprietary app phones home Unrestricted egress net none or filtered bridge + protocol unix,inet Ransomware-ish writer Encrypts all of ~ read-only ~ + whitelist ~/Share → nowhere to write ■ L0 CHECKPOINT — pass 2/3 to unlock L1 1. What does the firejail binary use its SUID-root moment for? To run your app as root forever To build namespaces/mounts/filters, then drop to your UID To install packages automatically 2. Which command lists/jailed processes? firemon --list firejail --uninstall chmod 777 ~ 3. Paranoid-first PDF viewing looks like… evince secret.pdf as root disabling your firewall firejail --net=none --private evince secret.pdf GRADE & UNLOCK L1 ▸ ★ L0 CLEARED ★ LEVEL 1 The six walls — Linux namespaces CLEARANCE: WATCHER • PREREQ: L0 🔒 SEALED — clear Level 0 to break this seal. A namespace gives a process a private view of one kernel resource. Same kernel, different lies. Firejail's default sandbox always takes mount + PID + UTS ; you add net, IPC, user for paranoia. 🧱 MNT — private filesystem table (always on) 👁 PID — jailed app is PID 1, cannot see host processes 🏷 UTS — fake hostname (no fingerprinting your box) 📡 IPC — no shared memory / semaphores with host 🌐 NET — private network stack (--net=none / --net=eth0) 🧤 USER — map you to nobody, fake root (--noroot) 🔥 YOUR APP (thinks it owns the machine) mnt ✓ pid ✓ uts ✓ ipc ✕ net ✕ user ✕ Click a layer… ☠ ENABLE FULL PARANOIA (all six) # See the lies yourself firejail --noprofile --ipc --net=none --private bash ps aux # only jail processes! hostname; ip a # fake/lo-only world ls /proc/1/exe # your shell, not systemd exit ☠ Paranoid rule: always add ipc-namespace , net none (or filtered net ), and noroot unless the app provably needs otherwise. Defaults are sane; paranoia is six walls, not three. ■ L1 CHECKPOINT — pass 2/3 1. Which namespaces are on by default? net + user + ipc mount + PID + UTS only seccomp 2. Inside a PID namespace, the jailed shell sees… itself as PID 1, host processes hidden all host processes as usual no processes at all 3. --noroot does what? disables firejail gives the app real root user-namespace with no root inside the jail GRADE & UNLOCK L2 ▸ ★ L1 CLEARED ★ LEVEL 2 Files & contexts — what "visible" really means CLEARANCE: ARCHIVIST • PREREQ: L1 🔒 SEALED — clear Level 1 first. 2.1 Four layers of "file context" — do not confuse them A file's context is every answer to "who may do what with it, and who decides?" A paranoid operator reads all four: # Context layer Decided by Example Firejail changes it? 1 DAC — classic Unix owner/group/mode + ACLs filesystem bits -rw------- alice alice ~/.ssh/id_rsa No — but jail can hide the file entirely 2 xattr / MAC label — SELinux context, AppArmor attachment kernel policy unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 , ls -Z No — labels still enforced inside the jail 3 Firejail view — blacklist / whitelist / read-only / private profile blacklist ~/.ssh , whitelist ~/Docs Yes — this is the whole level 4 Landlock / sandbox extras — unprivileged per-process FS rules profile + kernel landlock.enforce + landlock.fs.read /tmp Yes (experimental, additive) ⚠️ Key truth: blacklist ≠ SELinux relabeling. Firejail shapes the view ; SELinux/AppArmor still judge every surviving access. They stack. Check both: ls -l and ls -Z . SELinux context anatomy (real example) $ ls -Z ~/Docs/secret.pdf unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 ~/Docs/secret.pdf │ │ │ └─ level (MLS: s0 = lowest) │ │ └─ type (policy rules target THIS) │ └─ role (which roles may touch it) └─ SELinux user (not your login name!) # Change it persistently via policy, never bare chcon on production: semanage fcontext -a -t user_home_t "$HOME/Docs(/.*)?" restorecon -Rv ~/Docs 2.2 Firejail's file directives — the complete arsenal Directive Jailed app sees… Writes survive? Does a Firejail whitelist grant SELinux permission by itself? yes, it relabels files no — SELinux policy still applies inside the jail GRADE & UNLOCK L3 ▸ ★ L2 CLEARED ★ LEVEL 3 Syscalls, capabilities & no-new-privs CLEARANCE: WARDEN • PREREQ: L2 🔒 SEALED — clear Level 2 first. Namespaces hide things. seccomp-bpf hides abilities . Every exploit finally begs the kernel via a syscall ( open, execve, ptrace, mount, socket, keyctl… ). Firejail installs a BPF filter that kills the process if it touches a forbidden one — for the app and all its children . ▶ DROP DEFAULT BLACKLIST (~300 blocked) ▶ DROP PARANOID (seccomp + memory-deny-write-execute) ■ stop ▲ syscalls fall from the app ▬ BPF filter ▼ survivors reach the kernel 🟥 blocked → process killed 🟩 allowed → reaches kernel stats: — # The paranoid stack (add AFTER reading the shipped profile!) seccomp # default blacklist (~300 dangerous calls) seccomp.block-secondary # kill 32-bit compat ABI abuse memory-deny-write-execute # no W+X mappings: breaks JIT shellcode restrict-namespaces # app may not create new namespaces protocol unix,inet,inet6 # no bluetooth, raw packet, etc. caps.drop all nonewprivs noroot # scalpel instead of hammer, when you know the app: # seccomp.keep read,write,open,openat,close,fstat,mmap,brk,exit_group ☠ Paranoid order of operations: seccomp first, then caps.drop all , then nonewprivs + noroot . Capabilities without nonewprivs still let a setuid helper re-escalate. Verify with firemon --seccomp --caps . ■ L3 CHECKPOINT — pass 2/3 1. seccomp-bpf filters… which syscalls the jailed tree may invoke (inherited by children) which websites you may visit your desktop wallpaper 2. nonewprivs means… run everything as root setuid/file-cap execs gain no new privilege (NO_NEW_PRIVS) disable passwords 3. memory-deny-write-execute hurts which attacker technique most? phishing emails weak passwords JIT-spray / writing then executing shellcode pages GRADE & UNLOCK L4 ▸ ★ L3 CLEARED ★ LEVEL 4 Network namespaces — unplug or filter the jail CLEARANCE: SIGNAL • PREREQ: L3 🔒 SEALED — clear Level 3 first. A fresh network namespace is a machine with the cables pulled: only lo . From there you choose: stay dark ( net none — strongest), or re-attach through a filtered virtual cable ( --net=eth0 + --netfilter= ). 🌍 no jail (open LAN) 🕳 net none (dark) 🧱 net + netfilter (no LAN, web only) 🔥 JAILED APP firefox 🌐 TARGET 192.168.1.5 (your LAN) policy: — Pick a mode. Packets animate; the log explains the verdict. # Dark (media players, PDF, office): firejail --net=none evince secret.pdf # Filtered browser (profile snippet): net eth0 netfilter /etc/firejail/nolocal.net dns 9.9.9.9 protocol unix,inet,inet6 # nolocal.net drops 192.168/16, 10/8, 172.16/12, 127/8 egress # → internet works, printer/router snooping dies ⚠️ A net namespace alone is not a firewall. You are choosing a workspace, not a separate subscription. 03 — The cast How one prompt becomes a reviewed change Freebuff does not send your whole request through one giant prompt to one giant model. A coordinator reads the turn, decides which narrow specialists to spawn, gives each one only the context and permissions it needs, and stitches the results together. That is why the same product can find a file cheaply, reason expensively, run a shell command under supervision and review the diff before you ever see it. STEP 01 Intent You describe an outcome. The coordinator classifies the task: explore, edit, debug, research, or build. STEP 02 Context project-scout supplies the repo map; file-picker ranks the handful of files that actually matter. STEP 03 Plan For hard turns, thinker-with-files-gemini reads the relevant files and reasons on Gemini Pro before any edit. STEP 04 Execute The agent edits files and asks shell-runner for installs, builds and test commands inside a permission boundary. STEP 05 Verify test-runner runs only the relevant suite; browser-use drives Chromium when rendered behaviour matters. STEP 06 Review code-reviewer reads the diff by severity — regressions, missing tests, security smells — and sends fixes back. STEP 07 Deliver git-curator stages, writes a commit message in your repo's style, and opens a PR with /pr . STEP 08 Report You get the change, the commands that ran, the test output and any open risk — not just “done”. The nine subagents Who does what, and when they run Each has narrow scope, narrow context and narrow trust. You can call any of them by hand with /agent <name> . file-picker 01 Runs a fast Flash Lite model against a local code map to find the files that matter for the current task. Returns ranked paths plus a one-line justification for each. Almost every other subagent depends on it. Runs At the start of almost every turn · Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite code-reviewer 02 Reads diffs after an edit and reports issues by severity. Catches obvious regressions, missing tests and security smells. Its findings go back into the loop, not just into a report you have to act on manually. Runs Automatically after any multi-file edit · or /review browser-use 03 Drives a real Chromium instance to verify the app you just edited still works. Logs in, navigates, asserts on the rendered DOM, takes screenshots. Used heavily on full-stack tasks generated in the App Builder. Runs When behaviour in a browser is the acceptance test thinker-with-files-gemini 04 When a turn needs deep reasoning, the coordinator hands off. It reads the files it needs and thinks the problem through on Gemini Pro — included inside Freebuff rather than billed as a separate upgrade. Runs On architecture, tricky bugs and cross-file reasoning researcher 05 Does web research with citations. Useful when the task touches an unfamiliar library, a changed API or a version-specific behaviour. Returns a short brief with linked sources so you can check the claim. Runs On docs, releases and “how does this service work” turns test-runner 06 Detects the project's test framework — vitest, jest, pytest, go test, cargo test — and runs only the relevant tests instead of the whole suite. Streams failures back to the coordinator for repair. Runs After edits that can break behaviour git-curator 07 Stages, commits and writes commit messages that match the repository's historical style. Opens pull requests with /pr . Refuses to push to main unless you explicitly ask it to. Runs When you approve committing or opening a PR shell-runner 08 Executes shell commands inside a permission boundary. Destructive commands always require approval. Long-running processes are backgrounded with output streamed to a terminal file the main agent can read. Runs For installs, builds, servers, migrations and tests project-scout 09 Added in 2026. Indexes the repository on first run and keeps the index warm, tracking recent edits, build outputs, lint errors and stack metadata so the coordinator has fast structural understanding without re-reading the whole tree. Runs First run, then continuously in the background ⌘ Call the cast yourself Force a specialist with /agent file-picker , /review or /pr . If a subagent is noisy for a particular repo, disable it with --no-subagent <name> at startup or in .freebuffrc . ! Trust boundaries are real The reviewer does not get browser logs; the browser does not get shell history. The shell agent can refuse what the coordinator cannot. Destructive commands need your approval, and git will not push to main unasked. ◎ Cost-aware by design File discovery runs on a cheap, fast model. Expensive reasoning is reserved for turns that need it. That division is the reason an hour of Freebuff can cover a surprising amount of work. freedom: Freedom of Choice FreeBSD vs Gentoo Have you ever installed Gentoo Linux ? If you ever did, then you know how much pain you pass through just to have your Linux box ready to serve your needs. Gentoo installation is a learning process and the worst of it, is when you need to update, which needs to be something like once per week. If you take longer, you will find some USE=“flags” problems in the process, while many other problems can happen before you even boot it from the first time. I encourage you to try, mainly if you are a big FAN of memory usage performance and CPU performance too. Compilation time is your best friend, and hopefully you know to leave the computer away for some time, when compiling software. For exemple, to compile GCC that may take several hours. Anyway, when you boot your Gentoo for the first time, in case you already compile the kernel from the source , which you specify which hardware you have and which software compability you wish to have, the software you install, will be at its best, for your machine characteristics . In the other hand, in the last years, Gentoo implement Binary packages, to save your Time . While Time is saved, you cannot change the default configuration of the package you install, because was made to have all features , not only those you need. By default in FreeBSD , you may wish to use ZFS partition shema. It will take some memory from you, but if memory is not a problem, continue with ZFS. If Memory is a problem, please choose UFS . With FreeBSD , installation is super easy and no problems will come for installing it in your machine (mostly). After that super-fast installation, you can think you are using Gentoo. FreeBSD ports have everything you need to start. Use the whereis command, to find the programs you wish to install and go into that directory, and install them all, using the make command. But wait, before installing anything you should compile the kernel . The kernel you are using is generic and what you need is only the code that make your hardware work. All other hardware devices that you don’t have or use, can be removed, which will results in a faster kernel. You can start with GCC if you wish, to remember how much time it takes in Gentoo , while FreeBSD will ask you so many questions in the process of installing one single software, that you can quit from installing it from the source. Even if you can use pkg package to install the binary versions, you can escape that annoying problem with make BATCH=yes install clean , but keep in mind that some packages have non-desired features included, so you may wish to investigate the Makefile of each package you wish to install, to be sure that you will not install, what you don’t need. For example Vim will install the X server. In my perspective this is completly insane, but what can I do against it? Offend FreeBSD developers :) So remove the gtk2 , gtk3 , motif and x11 from Makefile . This is about the /usr/ports/editors/vim package, but others can have different packages that you don’t need. For example samba or smb , which is to manage Window$ filesystems, telnet which is a non-secure communication, while can be useful, you can try the secure approach, using ssh . To simplify the problem of editing the Makefile , use the command make config . As another popular example you may wish to install in case you are building a server is Apache2 . You may wish to remove all the CGI modules to be sure that have no known vulnerabilities. Another awesome feature is that, some packages can be Flagged as Vulnerable , mainly when you are trying to compile them from the source. If this happen, compilation will break / stop and some message will be described to “jump off” the problem, which is by adding the option: make DISABLE_VULNERABILITIES=yes install clean to continue. I am not sure about the sensation I have when compiling from source, but I think the compilation time is less than Gentoo, while I need to tell you the true: The Truth is, I start compilation and leave computer for some time. The Bike and the Road are always good friends to forget Time. In case you wish to install something that have deeper dependencies, you may wish to use the command make config-recursive , to select the compatibilities of all dependencies, before compiling them. If you think this ncurses-popups are annoying, try to make install clean without any extra option, and you will see the hugly side of FreeBSD ports . To enable services that you install at boot time , like the ssh-server , you need to add it to the /etc/rc.conf file. For example: apache24_enable=“YES” or dbus_enable="NO" , ssh_enable="YES" , etc. So, the lesson of using FreeBSD is to use this last tips before installing each package from /usr/ports/ . And always clean . If you like to explore more, please check the Jail system and the PF Firewall. If you wish to build a Desktop , I should remember you that the list of packages to install is Big . This article is like a motivation to learn more about FreeBSD freedom. I don’t really care about the licenses , but the usability that gives an opportunity of it’s experience. Nothing more. funnyReactions: How Frustrated they will feel In the article Being Fair I told you that all attackers IPs will be redirected to Wikipedia. To change your IP you need to stay without Internet for some hours. So, I imagine how Frustrated they will feel when they discover that they need to change IPs to access this website again. :) The logic of the redirect A block has a problem: it tells the attacker that he was seen, and a blocked address is a small obstacle for anyone with a list of proxies. A redirect has a much better property, it gives the visitor exactly what he asked for and nothing that he wanted. He asked to read a page, and he receives a page. He asked for a login form, and he receives an article about logic. The request succeeds, the log is clean, and the only thing that failed is the intention behind the request, which was never mine to satisfy. Why Wikipedia Because it is useful, it is free, and it is the opposite of a target. If you are going to send a robot somewhere, send it somewhere it can learn something. Maybe the address that spent an hour probing for a database will spend ten minutes reading about databases. That would be a far better result than any ban. And there is the joke inside the joke: the more they insist, the more they read. Somewhere out there is an automated script that has now visited more articles about philosophy than most humans do in a lifetime. The honest part I do not hate the attackers. I dislike the noise they make. What I really dislike is the idea that a site has to be defended with anger, with threat, with a page that says your IP was recorded and the police are coming . That is theatre, and poor theatre, because nothing happens and everybody knows it. So I chose the version with a smile. The frustrated one is not the reader, and it is not me. :)

Level 00 The mental model What Git actually stores, why a commit is not a diff, and why hashes explain almost every confusing message you will ever see. 1. A version control system written in ten days In 2005 the Linux kernel project lost its free BitKeeper licence. Linus Torvalds needed a replacement with properties the existing tools did not offer: it had to be fast, fully distributed, and resistant to corruption. He wrote the first version of Git in roughly ten days; the first kernel commit landed in April 2005, and Git has been versioning its own source ever since. That origin explains its personality: Git was designed for a project with thousands of contributors, enormous trees, and no tolerance for silent data loss. Nearly every design decision that surprises beginners follows from that history. Git is not “SVN with extra commands”. It is a content-addressed object database with a small porcelain layer on top. The porcelain — commit , branch , merge — is what you use daily; the database is what makes recovery, hashing, and distributed work possible. The one-sentence model Git is a key–value store where the key is the SHA hash of the content, and a repository is a directed acyclic graph of commit objects that point at trees of blobs. 2. Snapshots, not deltas Most version control systems store a base file plus a chain of changes. Git stores a snapshot of the entire tree for each commit. When a file has not changed between commits, the new tree simply points at the same blob that the previous tree pointed at. Nothing is duplicated; unchanged files cost one hash reference, not a copy. Question Delta-based VCS Git What is stored per revision? Instructions to transform the previous revision A complete tree of content hashes Cost of an unchanged file Usually nothing One pointer to an existing blob Checking out an old revision Replay changes forward or backward Materialise one tree Corruption detection Depends on the backend Every object is verified against its hash Branch cost Often a server-side copy One 41-byte file pointing at a commit Because the snapshot is the unit, comparing two commits is a computation, not a stored artefact. git diff A B walks two trees and reports differences. That is also why a merge conflict is a text problem: Git has three snapshots and must propose a combined tree. 3. The three trees Everyday Git is the art of moving changes between three places. Confusing them is the source of most “Git ate my work” reports. WORKING TREE INDEX / STAGING HEAD / COMMIT GRAPH ────────────── ───────────────── ──────────────────── hello.txt (v2, saved) ──add──▶ hello.txt (v2) ──commit──▶ tree + parent + metadata │ │ │ └── edits you have not staged └── exactly what the next └── immutable once written live only here commit will contain Tree What it is Where it lives Command that inspects it Working tree Real files on disk, including untracked and ignored ones Your project directory git status , git diff Index The proposed next commit — a binary file, not a folder .git/index git diff --staged , git ls-files -s HEAD Ref pointing at the current commit on the current branch .git/HEAD git log -1 , git show HEAD Watch the distinction in real output. Create a file, stage it, then edit it again: $ git init demo && cd demo $ printf 'one
' > hello.txt $ git add hello.txt $ printf 'two
' >> hello.txt $ git status --short AM hello.txt A in the first column means added to the index; M in the second means modified again in the working tree. The index holds version one; the disk holds version two. git commit would capture version one. This is not a bug — it is the staging area letting you commit a coherent subset of a messy afternoon. 4. Everything is an object A Git repository contains exactly four object types. All are compressed with zlib and addressed by the SHA hash of their contents. blob File content The bytes of a file. No name, no permissions, no path. A blob is purely content. tree Directory listing An ordered list of names, modes, and object hashes. Trees can point at other trees, forming directories. commit Snapshot + provenance One tree hash, zero or more parents, author and committer identities with timestamps, and a message. tag Annotated label A signed or unsigned object that points at another object with a message. Used for releases. The hash is not random and not assigned by a server. It is computed from the object's type, its byte length, and its content. Hashing the three bytes hello plus a newline always produces the same identifier: $ printf 'hello
' | git hash-object --stdin ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a $ git cat-file -t ce0136 blob $ git cat-file -p ce0136 hello Two consequences follow, and they explain a great deal of Git behaviour: Identical content is stored once. Ten branches with the same README.md share one blob. Changing anything changes the hash. A commit hash covers the tree and every parent, so changing an old commit changes every descendant hash. This is why rebase and amend produce “new” commits even when the diff looks the same. Inspect any repository without checking it out git cat-file -p <hash> pretty-prints any object. git cat-file -s <hash> prints its size. git rev-parse HEAD resolves a name to a hash. These three plumbing commands turn Git from magic into something you can query. 5. Branches are labels; tags are labels that stay put A branch is a file under .git/refs/heads/ containing a commit hash. Creating a branch writes 41 bytes. Switching branches moves HEAD and updates the working tree. Committing on a branch writes a new commit and then rewrites that one small file. That is the entire mechanism — branch operations are cheap because they are pointer operations. $ cat .git/HEAD ref: refs/heads/main $ git rev-parse main 4f3c1a9d2e5b7c0a8d6e4f2b1c3a5e7d9b0f2a4c $ git branch -a * main feature/login remotes/origin/main Annotated tags are objects too, with their own hash, tagger, date, message, and optional signature. A lightweight tag is just a ref pointing directly at a commit. Use annotated tags for releases: they carry metadata and can be verified with git tag -v . Detached HEAD is a state, not an error If HEAD contains a raw hash instead of ref: refs/heads/… , you are “detached”: commits you make belong to no branch and will be unreachable once you leave, unless you create a branch. Nothing is lost immediately — the reflog keeps it for weeks — but Level 06 shows exactly how to rescue it. 6. What Git deliberately does not do Knowing the non-features prevents whole categories of bad architecture. Git is not a general-purpose file system or a deployment system. Not tracked Empty directories Git stores files, not folders. A directory with no files does not exist in the object model. The conventional workaround is a placeholder .gitkeep . Barely tracked Permissions Only the executable bit survives. Ownership, ACLs, extended attributes, and timestamps are not versioned. Inferred Renames Git stores no rename records. It detects renames at diff time by similarity. A rename plus heavy edits may appear as delete + add, which is why history can look broken. No locking Concurrent edits Git has no file locks. Two people can edit the same file; conflicts surface at merge time. Git LFS adds opt-in locking for binaries. Not a backup Disaster recovery A push is not a backup. History rewrites, force pushes, and account deletion are all possible. Mirror to a second host and take real backups. Not a deploy tool Release delivery Git transports source. Deploying by git pull on a production server is a classic anti-pattern; Level 10 explains why in detail. 7. Distributed means every clone is a repository There is no privileged copy. origin is not special; it is a nickname for a URL, created by git clone . You can commit, branch, merge, and inspect history on a plane with no network. Synchronisation is a separate, explicit act: fetch downloads objects, push uploads them, and pull is fetch plus integration. $ git remote -v origin git@github.com:ada/demo.git (fetch) origin git@github.com:ada/demo.git (push) $ git remote add backup https://gitlab.com/ada/demo.git $ git remote -v backup https://gitlab.com/ada/demo.git (fetch) backup https://gitlab.com/ada/demo.git (push) This is what makes multi-host resilience trivial: add a second remote and push the same refs to it. Identify the tree hash, the parent (absent on the first commit), and the author/committer lines. Run git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree} and then git cat-file -p <blob-hash> . You just walked commit → tree → blob. Run git count-objects -v and compare count with the number of files you created. Explain the extra objects. Delete the working file with rm , then restore it with git restore <file> . Note that the blob was never touched — only the working tree was. What you are actually installing “Git” is a command-line program plus a set of helper executables: git-commit , git-remote-https , git-credential-manager , and so on. On Windows you also get a POSIX emulation layer (Git Bash) and a credential manager. On macOS the system ships a stub that prompts you to install the Command Line Tools. On Linux you get whatever version your distribution froze at release time — sometimes years old. The practical rule: install the newest stable Git your platform makes easy, then verify which binary your shell actually resolves. Most “this flag doesn't exist” problems are a second, older Git earlier in PATH . 2. Before you install: environment checks Five minutes of preparation prevents most installation support tickets. The goal is to know which Git you are installing, who can install it, and whether the machine can reach the network through whatever proxy and certificate authority your organisation uses. Check Why it matters How to confirm Administrator rights System installers need elevation; per-user installs do not sudo -v (macOS/Linux) or an elevated PowerShell Package manager health A stale index installs an old Git or fails outright apt update , brew update , winget source list Proxy and TLS inspection Git uses libcurl; a corporate proxy without its CA bundle breaks clones curl -I https://github.com Disk space Source builds and large repositories need room for objects and packs df -h or Get-PSDrive Filesystem behaviour Case-insensitive or symlink-hostile filesystems change checkout behaviour Windows: long paths and Developer Mode; macOS: case-insensitive APFS Existing configuration An old ~/.gitconfig may override your new defaults git config --list --show-origin # What is already installed, and from where? which -a git 2>/dev/null || where git git --version 2>/dev/null # Back up existing configuration before changing anything cp ~/.gitconfig ~/.gitconfig.backup 2>/dev/null || true git config --list --show-origin > ~/git-config-before.txt 2>/dev/null # Corporate proxy and custom CA (never disable verification) git config --global http.proxy http://proxy.corp.example:8080 git config --global https.proxy http://proxy.corp.example:8080 git config --global http.sslCAInfo /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/corp-root.crt git config --global http.sslVerify true # macOS: accept the Xcode licence non-interactively if you use the CLT Git sudo xcodebuild -license accept # Debian/Ubuntu: CA certificates and build prerequisites sudo apt update && sudo apt install ca-certificates http.sslVerify false is not a fix Disabling TLS verification turns every clone and fetch into an unauthenticated download. If a proxy intercepts traffic, install its root certificate and point http.sslCAInfo at the bundle. The same rule applies to GIT_SSL_NO_VERIFY : it is a debugging flag, not a configuration. If your organisation mandates a specific version, signing policy, or credential helper, settle that before installing. Replacing a package-manager Git with a source build later is easy; untangling repositories created with the wrong line-ending or signing settings is not. O brasão oficial foi aprovado pela Portaria n.º 129/73; este desenho não substitui o símbolo institucional. 01 · SIMBOLOGIA O dragão de duas cabeças O brasão da Guarda Nacional Republicana é um escudo verde. Ao centro, uma espada antiga de ouro. Seguram-na dois dragões afrontados, também de ouro, animados, lampassados e armados de vermelho. No timbre, um terceiro dragão empunha a mesma espada. A leitura oficial é curta e antiga: a espada representa o carácter castrense; os dragões, a defesa da lei e da grei. «Grei» é uma palavra que já quase ninguém usa. Designava o rebanho, o povo, a comunidade dos que precisam de guarda. Não é o Estado, nem o Governo, nem a nação abstracta: é o conjunto concreto de pessoas que dorme atrás daquela porta. A Portaria n.º 129/73, que aprovou o brasão, usa exactamente essa palavra: «grei». O dragão da GNR não guarda um tesouro; guarda uma promessa. Na tradição europeia, o dragão é quase sempre o monstro. Guarda o ouro, devora o herói, exige donzelas. É a fera que São Jorge mata. O dragão da GNR pertence a essa família visual, mas foi domesticado pela burocracia: continua a ter dentes, garras e língua de fogo, mas está dentro de um escudo, com uma espada na pata. É a força que se deixou encerrar num regulamento. A pergunta de todo o dossiê é esta: o que acontece quando o regulamento falha e a fera fica sozinha? Na Ásia, o dragão é outra gramática. O lóng chinês não é o monstro que cospe fogo sobre aldeias; é a água que fecunda, a nuvem que traz a chuva, o yang que organiza o mundo. É um dos quatro animais auspiciosos, com o fénix, o qilin e a tartaruga. Pode ser imperial — o imperador era o Filho do Céu e o dragão de cinco garras era o seu emblema —, mas também é o animal que representa a sabedoria que atravessa o tempo. No Japão, o ryū habita rios e mares; na Coreia, o yong protege o céu; no Vietname, o rồng é fundador e guardião. Em toda a Ásia, o dragão não pede culto: pede discernimento. Há uma cena que resume esta outra metade. Segundo o Shiji de Sima Qian, Confúcio visitou Laozi e voltou perturbado. Disse aos discípulos: «Sei como voam os pássaros, como nadam os peixes, como correm os animais. Sei caçá-los. Mas o dragão, não sei: sobe nas nuvens e no vento até ao céu. Hoje vi Laozi. Não será ele semelhante ao dragão?» O dragão, aqui, não é o inimigo a abater. É o limite do entendimento, a forma que a sabedoria toma quando já não cabe numa definição. O dragão da GNR tem, por isso, duas cabeças. Uma morde — é a força legítima, a intervenção, a detenção, o último recurso. A outra pensa — é o discernimento, a proporcionalidade, a recusa da ordem injusta, o cuidado com quem está do outro lado da farda. Uma instituição sem a primeira é uma promessa sem meios. Uma instituição sem a segunda é uma espada sem punho. A força sem sabedoria é tirania. A sabedoria sem força é impotência. O dragão completo é a tensão entre as duas — nunca o equilíbrio definitivo. Tese deste dossiê O blog já tinha escrito sobre este animal antes de a GNR entrar nesta página. Em A Lenda do Macaco Dragão , o dragão é «a sabedoria ancestral, silenciosa e profunda do espírito»; em Dragon Fire (龙火) , a palavra é fogo que pode ferir; em Monkey Memories , «o Dragão esteve sempre lá como guardião e protector eterno». E o Tao lembra que a força que se dobra também governa. Não é estranho, portanto, que a Guarda use um dragão. Estranho seria se o usasse apenas para assustar. 02 · 1801–1911 A longa gestação de uma polícia militar Antes de haver GNR, houve medo. Lisboa crescia sem iluminação, sem polícia profissional e sem aquilo a que hoje chamaríamos inteligência criminal. Em 1801, o príncipe regente D. João aprovou a criação da Guarda Real da Polícia, por proposta do intendente Pina Manique. O modelo veio de França: a Gendarmerie , criada em 1791, era uma força militar com funções policiais, precisamente para garantir que a ordem não dependesse apenas de milícias locais. Portugal copiou a ideia com uma exigência de elite: os melhores soldados do Exército, solteiros, robustos, até aos 30 anos, de «boa morigeração e conduta». A Guarda não nasceu para ser querida. Nasceu para ser respeitada. O regulamento dizia que o corpo devia ser «uma Força Nacional, que segure a tranquilidade interna da Capital». A frase é reveladora: a capital, não o país. Durante décadas, a polícia de Lisboa e a do Porto foram instituições separadas, com lógicas próprias, ciúmes próprios e uma relação difícil com o poder político. 1801 A cidade e o medo A Guarda Real da Polícia de Lisboa é criada por influência de Pina Manique, inspirada na Gendarmerie francesa. É um corpo de elite, com funções de polícia e organização militar. A experiência de 1793, com uma companhia militar de polícia, tinha sido o ensaio. 1807 A corte parte, a Guarda fica Com a invasão francesa, a família real embarca para o Brasil. A Guarda permanece em Lisboa e o seu comandante, o conde de Novion, colabora com Junot. Alguns oficiais e soldados juntam-se ao exército português; 41 deles combatem no Vimeiro, onde o seu capitão morre. A instituição aprende cedo a lição mais incómoda: servir o Estado não é o mesmo que servir o regime. 1834 A factura da fidelidade No fim da guerra civil, a Guarda Real é extinta por ter estado do lado de D. Miguel. Nasce a Guarda Municipal de Lisboa e a do Porto, com características semelhantes. Em 1868, as duas passam a ter um comando-geral unificado no Quartel do Carmo, o mesmo edifício que ainda hoje é a sede da GNR. 1910 A última força monárquica A Guarda Municipal é a última força monárquica a render-se aos republicanos. A ironia é quase literária: a instituição que resistiu à República é renomeada Guarda Republicana e, no ano seguinte, recebe o nome que ainda hoje tem. Há um fio que atravessa estes primeiros cem anos: a Guarda serve quem está no poder, mas sobrevive à queda de quem está no poder. Muda de nome, de farda, de tutela e de juramento. O que não muda é a quadrícula: a presença capilar no território, o conhecimento do terreno, a capacidade de estar onde a polícia urbana não chega. É essa continuidade que explica por que razão a GNR de 2026 ainda se reconhece na Guarda de 1801, apesar de tudo o que mudou. 03 · 1911–2026 A Guarda no século que mudou tudo Em 3 de maio de 1911, um decreto cria a Guarda Nacional Republicana. A fórmula é a que ainda hoje define a instituição: militares organizados num corpo especial de tropas, dependentes do ministério da segurança pública em tempo de paz e do ministério militar para a doutrina, o armamento e o equipamento. Em guerra ou crise grave, passam para o comando operacional das Forças Armadas. É uma dupla natureza que nunca deixou de ser uma dupla tensão. O aniversário da Guarda é 3 de maio; a patrona é Nossa Senhora do Carmo. Durante o Estado Novo, a Guarda foi chamada a garantir a ordem pública, escoltar autoridades e proteger instalações. Como todas as forças de ordem de um regime autoritário, não esteve fora da política: esteve dentro dela, com o dever de obedecer e a margem de discricionariedade que qualquer policiamento de rua contém. Essa é uma parte da história que a instituição não deve apagar, porque é exactamente o que permite compreender o 25 de Abril. Na manhã de 25 de Abril de 1974, Marcelo Caetano refugiou-se no Quartel do Carmo, sede do Comando-Geral da GNR. Ali foi cercado pelas forças de Salgueiro Maia e ali se rendeu. A ditadura terminou dentro da casa da Guarda. A cena tem uma força simbólica que nenhum brasão consegue resumir: a instituição que tinha guardado o regime foi também o último tecto do regime, e sobreviveu ao regime que caiu. Nos anos seguintes, a democracia reconstruiu a tutela, a fiscalização e o mandato. A GNR passou a depender do Ministério da Administração Interna, com uma ligação militar ao Ministério da Defesa. Em 1993, a Guarda absorveu a Guarda Fiscal, criada em 1885. Não foi uma fusão administrativa: foi a entrada da GNR no mundo dos impostos, das alfândegas, do contrabando e da criminalidade económica. Em 2006, integrou o Corpo Nacional da Guarda Florestal e reforçou o SEPNA, o Serviço de Protecção da Natureza e do Ambiente. A Guarda deixou de ser apenas a polícia das estradas e das aldeias; passou a ser também a polícia do dinheiro e da floresta. A reforma de 2007 — Lei n.º 63/2007 — redesenhou a estrutura. As antigas brigadas territoriais desapareceram, os comandos territoriais passaram a depender directamente do comando central e as unidades especializadas ganharam peso. A Brigada de Trânsito, que tinha sido uma das faces mais visíveis da GNR, foi extinta no processo; a sua estrutura central deu lugar à Unidade Nacional de Trânsito e os destacamentos passaram para os comandos territoriais. A extinção foi também uma resposta a escândalos de corrupção. Em 2018, o GIPS transformou-se na Unidade de Emergência de Protecção e Socorro, dando à Guarda uma capacidade própria de primeira intervenção em fogos rurais. Em 2026, o Governo anunciou o regresso da Brigada de Trânsito. A nova unidade deveria nascer «nos moldes da antiga», com cerca de 1 300 militares na fase inicial e rotação de funções para prevenir corrupção. Até ao fecho deste dossiê, em 23 de outubro de 2026, não havia data de arranque anunciada, nem lei orgânica alterada, nem sede definida. A reforma estava anunciada; a instituição ainda não existia. É uma diferença que este artigo não quer apagar. A Guarda aprendeu a sobreviver mudando de nome, de tutela e de inimigo. O que a manteve igual foi a quadrícula: estar em todo o lado antes de ser chamada. Uma hipótese sobre 225 anos de continuidade Há, claro, uma leitura menos generosa. Uma instituição que sobrevive a todos os regimes pode ser vista como uma instituição que se adapta a todos os poderes. A resposta a essa acusação não está no brasão nem na cronologia; está naquilo que a Guarda faz quando a ordem política colide com a lei. É aí que o dragão mostra se guarda a grei ou apenas a espada. 04 · ESTRUTURA O mapa da Guarda — comandos, unidades e serviços A GNR é uma força de segurança com natureza e organização militares. Não se organiza em «divisões» como um exército em campanha. Organiza-se em comandos, unidades e serviços, com uma lógica simples: cobrir o território, especializar o que exige técnica e concentrar no centro aquilo que não pode ser improvisado. The mirror image History books are full of evil done in the name of Good. This page is about the reverse: good done by people the system called evil. Deserters who would not shoot . Clerks who lost the file . Officers who warned the village. Policemen who opened the gate instead of closing it. They were rarely heroes in uniform. They were usually quiet, afraid and alone. That is why their acts matter more than medals. The machine asked for one more name, one more signature, one more silence. They gave none of the three. 2. Those who refused Refusal rarely looks like a speech. It looks like delay, like a lost order , like a truck that breaks down on the way to the roundup , like a warning passed in a whisper. Small acts, multiplied, saved streets, families and sometimes whole towns. The order was made not to be questioned. They questioned it anyway. 3. Soldiers who said no In every war there were men who would not fire on civilians , pilots who reported false coordinates , conscripts who carried the wounded of the other side. Courts punished many of them. History acquitted almost all of them. Their lesson is simple: a uniform does not remove choice. It only raises its price. 4. Police who protected Police who refused to beat, who refused to plant evidence, who registered the complaint against their own colleagues. Those files teach justice only when someone dares to police the police. They were called disloyal. Communities remember them by name decades later, while the obedient are forgotten. Protection, not punishment, is what the badge was supposed to mean. 5. The price of disobedience Doing good inside an evil machine is expensive: demotion, prison, exile, sometimes death. That is why it is rare, and why every case had to be decided alone, without applause, without knowing the ending. Evil in the name of Good is routine. A database query, a deportation signature, a body-camera switched off, a quota for fines. The modern refusal is also quiet: log the truth, keep the copy, demand the order in writing, tell someone outside the chain. 7. The grammar of a good cause The sentence is older than any of the states that use it: the cause is good, therefore the act is permitted . Every entry in this dossier is a version of that sentence, and the seven nouns that most often fill the first slot are these. The seven good names, with their classic instrument Good name What it authorises Typical work God, faith, the sacred Conversion, purification of belief, holy war Crusades, inquisitions, witch-hunting, forced baptism The nation, the fatherland Expansion, unification, ethnic purity Colonial conquest, partition, "ethnic cleansing" Order, security, the law Policing, emergency powers, anti-subversion Massacres of protest, dirty wars, body counts Purity, health, race Eugenics, sterilisation, extermination T4, forced sterilisations, genocides named as hygiene The people, the class, the revolution Class enemies, re-education, Year Zero Terror, collectivisation, killing fields Progress, civilisation, science Civilising missions, dispossession, experiments Colonies, boarding schools, human experimentation Peace, humanity, human rights Interventions, sanctions, drones, "humanitarian" war Wars sold as protection, prisons outside the law Two things must be said clearly, because this is the point where readers usually stop listening. First: none of these names is evil in itself. Faith, nation, order, health, justice, progress and peace are real goods, held honestly by billions of people, including the people in this file who refused to use them as a warrant. The dossier is not an argument against good causes. It is an argument against the conversion of a good cause into a permission — the moment the noun stops being a direction to walk in and becomes a reason why this particular body does not count. Second: the mechanics are identical whether the good name is religious or secular. The crusader, the commissioner of a colony, the officer of a dictatorship, the interrogator of a democracy and the commander of a "humanitarian" war are not doing the same thing for the same reason, but they are using the same three instruments — an unexamined cause, a distance from the victim, and a word that hides the act while it happens. When a cause cannot be questioned, the act does not need to be justified. That is what a licence looks like. What follows is the file, and the file has a shape. In every century, in every continent, the same sequence appears: a real grievance or a real fear; a Good that promises to solve it; a category of people redefined as the obstacle; an institution that supplies trained men and paperwork; a word that makes the killing sayable at dinner; and, at the end, a court or a commission, sitting years later, with the receipt. 2. The anatomy of the act History is not written by the cause. It is written, or buried, by the fourth and fifth items in that sequence: the institution and the word. A cause needs an institution before it can kill A mob can murder; only an institution can organise a genocide. The organisational ingredients are boringly consistent, and the study of them is one of the few places where social science directly enters a courtroom: Division of labour — the person who makes the list is not the person who knocks on the door, and the person who drives is not the person who shoots. Each of them can say, truthfully, that he did not do the whole thing. Written criteria — a form, a quota, a category, a register. The Khmer Rouge photographed and catalogued every prisoner at S-21; the police battalions filed reports of their shootings; the colonial administrations counted the "effectifs". A paper trail is how you can later prove what a nation will spend decades denying. Distance — an office, a screen, a telephone, a border, an altitude. Distance is the cheapest anaesthetic ever invented, and it is administered in shifts. Euphemism — a word that hides the act while the act happens: pacification, resettlement, collateral damage, enhanced interrogation, Year Zero, final solution. Victor Klemperer's study of the language of the Third Reich and Orwell's essay on political language remain the two clearest catalogues of how this works, because words name the act to the person doing it. De-escalation Calm Presence Empathy Communication Prevention 1. The Philosophy of Good Policing A good police officer understands that most people in crisis are not looking for a fight. They are looking for safety, to be heard, or for someone to help them make sense of a moment that has spiralled beyond their control. The goal is not to win. The goal is to de-escalate, to protect dignity, and to guide the person to a calmer state where cooperation becomes possible again. Calm is contagious. So is panic. Choose which one you spread. 2. Calm Presence & Body Language Your presence speaks first Open posture — Uncross arms, keep hands visible and relaxed. Avoid towering over people. Appropriate distance — Respect personal space. Move closer gradually only as trust builds. Steady pace — Walk slowly, speak slowly. Urgency is the enemy of calm. Neutral expression — Concern without judgment. A relaxed face disarms tension. Eye contact — Natural, respectful. Don't stare down or avoid completely. 3. The Language of Reassurance Words that calm Acknowledge — "I can see this is upsetting for you." Validation reduces defensiveness. Name the situation — "I'm here to help. Can you tell me what you need right now?" Offer control — Give choices when possible: "Would you like to sit here or over there?" Use their name — If they share it, use it respectfully. It humanises. Keep it simple — Short sentences. Complex explanations increase anxiety. What to avoid Commands — "Calm down!" almost never works. Replace with requests. Arguing — You don't need to win the reality debate in a crisis moment. Labels — Avoid "crazy", "irrational" or accusatory language. Threats — Save them for true immediate danger. They escalate most of the time. 4. Dealing with Stress, Anxiety & Paranoia People in acute stress may misinterpret intentions. Paranoia often comes from fear, not malice. Your job is to reduce threat perception. Validate the feeling — "I understand you're scared right now." Don't argue with their fear. Be transparent — Explain what you're doing before doing it: "I'm going to ask for ID to help sort this out." Go slow — Reduce stimuli. Speak one-on-one if possible, away from crowds. Focus on needs — Ask "What do you need right now?" often reveals the real issue. Stay patient — Sometimes silence is more calming than words. Give space to process. 5. Gentle Distraction & Redirection A kind word, a simple question, or gentle redirection can shift focus away from whatever is driving the panic. Grounding — "Can you feel your feet on the ground?" or ask about something tangible. Normal conversation — Ask about something neutral: weather, a pet, where they're from. Human connection breaks tension. Offer water — A small act of care builds trust instantly. Walk together — Moving side by side is less confrontational than face-to-face posturing. Focus on the next small step — "Let's just focus on getting to a quieter spot first." 6. Firmness Without Aggression Kindness and boundaries are not opposites. You can be compassionate and clear about what is and isn't acceptable. Use "I" statements — "I need you to stay behind this line so I can keep everyone safe." State limits clearly — One limit at a time. Repeat calmly if needed. Offer alternatives — "You can't do X, but you can do Y." Follow through calmly — If enforcement is necessary, do it with minimal words and maximum respect. Preserve dignity — Even in restraint, treat people as human beings. 7. Self-Regulation for the Officer You cannot calm others if you are not managing yourself first. Breathe — Slow, deep breaths between interactions. Regulate your own heart rate. Check your tone — If you feel frustration rising, lower your volume. Take a pause — "Give me a moment" is perfectly professional. Debrief — Process difficult encounters with trusted colleagues. Suppressing takes a toll. Practice empathy without taking on — Care deeply, but protect your own wellbeing too. 8. Practical Exercises Active listening — Practice reflecting back: "So what I'm hearing is..." without jumping to solutions. Pause before responding — Count 2-3 seconds after someone speaks before you reply. Role-play scenarios — Practice with colleagues using anxious, confused, or paranoid personas. Voice modulation — Record yourself speaking calmly and adjust pitch/speed. Post-encounter review — Ask: Did I listen? Did I stay calm? Could I have done better? 9. Playfulness, Tricks & Magic Sometimes the most powerful tool in de-escalation isn't authority, it's humanity. A touch of playfulness can break tension, build rapport, and redirect a stressed or paranoid person without ever needing to raise your voice or reach for force. Why it works It breaks the power dynamic — Sharing a moment of play puts you on the same level as the person, rather than facing off against them. It shifts focus — Curiosity pulls attention away from whatever is fueling their anxiety or paranoia. It builds trust — A genuine smile or bit of humor shows you're human, not just an enforcer. It creates cooperation — People are far more willing to listen to someone they just laughed with. Practical techniques Appropriate humor — A light, self-deprecating joke can go a long way. Never mock the person or their situation. Simple magic tricks — A basic coin trick, vanishing pen, or making a key appear can instantly spark curiosity and calm even the most agitated person. Circle skills — Spinning a pen, doing a simple palm trick, or even light juggling can be mesmerizing. Often people will ask to see it again, giving you time to talk calmly. Playful redirection — Ask them to try to guess how a trick works. This engages their brain differently and pulls them out of their spiral. Storytelling — A funny, harmless story can distract without dismissing their feelings. Pair it with validation: "I know you're upset, but let me show you something quick..." Important guidelines Read the room — Playfulness only works if the person is not in immediate life-threatening crisis or actively violent. If they're in full fight mode, go back to calm presence and boundaries first. Keep it simple — You don't need to be a professional magician. The goal isn't perfection, it's connection. Stay authentic — If you don't feel natural doing it, don't force it. Your calm presence is still your greatest tool. Never use it to mock — Playfulness is to connect, never to belittle or trick someone into compliance through shame. Know when to switch back — Once they're calmer, transition back to the task at hand with respect and clarity. Sometimes a coin trick can do more for de-escalation than a raised voice ever could. 10. google_and_banks: Google vs Banks I take some much time to create an app (which is not complete, yet), and Google Payment is against payments that are not banks. My bank is against most payments that are from online companies, which include Google :) So, solving another problem with this kind of incompatibilities between giants: Application will not be in Google Store or Apple Store . ( Free for me and for everyone else) Binary ( .apk ) will be stored in Github releases. Solved. Two giants, one developer in the middle The two institutions disagree about who is allowed to move money, and neither of them needs to explain the disagreement to me. Google wants to process the payment inside its own store, the bank wants to process it as a bank transfer or not at all, and the developer is the person who discovers the conflict only after the application is finished. There is no argument to win here. A rule that exists to protect a business model will not change because a small project is inconvenient, and a bank that distrusts online companies will not change because the company is famous. What a store really adds A store adds discovery, an update channel and a payment system. For a free application the first two are nice but not essential, and the third costs a percentage of a price that does not exist. What remains is a signature, a file, and a place where people can find it. That place can be a release page. The file can be downloaded directly, checked, and installed by whoever decides to trust it. The user loses the convenience of a single button and gains the ability to keep a copy, which in the long term is the same thing as an archive. The trade I accepted No store means no payment integration, no commission, no approval queue and no policy change that can remove the application overnight. It also means no visibility, and I accept that too. The people who need the tool will find the repository, and the ones who need a store will find another tool. Solved, as the text says. Not because the giants agreed, but because the path between them turned out to be open.
